One surprising commodity could benefit from the AI boom
World Gold Council’s Joe Cavatoni says gold’s role in chips and advanced technology could expand alongside the rapidly growing AI industry.
Investors have long prized gold as a hedge against inflation and economic uncertainty , but one of the world’s fastest-growing industries is now fueling a new source of demand for the precious metal.
The buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) is driving investment in advanced semiconductors, servers and the sprawling data centers needed to power the technology. That expansion also requires a range of materials used in high-performance electronics, including gold.
And the AI boom is creating a growing need at a time when gold is already historically expensive. Despite those high prices, tech companies aren't necessarily switching to cheaper materials — suggesting demand for golf could continue to grow alongside AI.
A QUIET RUSH FOR GOLD IS SWEEPING THE GLOBE — HERE'S WHY COUNTRIES ARE STOCKPILING IT
Gold is used in advanced semiconductors and electronics that help power the growing artificial intelligence industry. (Oscar Del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images)
Gold is valued in electronics for its conductivity, reliability and resistance to corrosion — and its role in some technology applications is proving resilient despite trading at roughly $4,153 an ounce on Oct. 5, up nearly 6%, or about $225, from a year earlier.
Joseph Cavatoni, a gold market expert and senior market strategist for North America at the World Gold Council, said companies would typically consider cheaper alternatives after developing technology that relies on gold.
"They might pioneer a technology with gold involved and then say, ‘Let’s find something cheaper like tungsten to replace it,’" Cavatoni told Fox News Digital. "But what we’re finding in this case is they’re not."
ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM
The artificial intelligence boom is fueling demand for advanced chips, servers and data centers, creating a growing need for materials such as gold. (Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images)
Technology demand is already showing signs of growth. Gold demand from the sector rose 2% from a year earlier to 80.4 metric tons in the second quarter, according to the World Gold Council. Electronics demand climbed 4% to 68.3 tons, fueled by AI infrastructure, high-end semiconductors and advanced components.
Cavatoni said gold can offer advantages over substitutes in applications such as chip production and heat conduction. The AI sector may also be less sensitive to elevated gold prices because relatively small amounts of the metal are needed.
"This is a rapidly growing space that’s less sensitive to price," Cavatoni said. "It’s going to likely continue to grow as the AI space grows."
Gold is used in advanced semiconductor chips because of its conductivity and reliability, making the precious metal an important material in the hardware powering the AI boom. (Doug Jones/Portland Press Herald/Getty Images)
Still, technology remains a small part of the overall gold market compared with investment, central-bank buying and jewelry. Cavatoni said it is "less likely to be a driver of the price of gold."
For now, Cavatoni described technology as an increasingly important contributor to gold demand that "doesn’t appear to be slowing down anytime soon."

items.content:
Image caption, Two injured crew members from one of the ships have been sent for treatment
A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.
A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued.
Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".
Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.
The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.
It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.
A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched.
Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.
Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.
Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".
He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."
He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.
"Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."
Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.
A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Russia-Ukraine war: Lithuania backs push to lift ban on nuclear arms
The Kremlin warned Lithuania’s moves toward allowing nuclear weapons and potentially hosting a permanent U.S. military base would mark a “significant escalation” of regional tensions.
Lithuania is seeking to bolster its security amid growing concerns over Russia, with Trump saying he would consider the NATO ally’s request for a permanent U.S. base.
Gitanas Nauseda, Lithuania's president, during the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026.
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned a preliminary decision by Lithuanian lawmakers to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and the potential deployment of a NATO military base in the country will mark "another significant escalation" of regional tensions.
The comments come shortly after Lithuania's parliament voted in favor of advancing a constitutional change on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory. It is the first of two ballots required for the change, with the latter scheduled for Jan. 12 next year.
The country, which is a member of both the European Union and NATO and shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea, has been looking to remove the constitutional ban to strengthen its resilience amid growing security concerns.
Lithuania has been one of Ukraine's staunchest allies during Russian President  Vladimir Putin 's more than 4½-year conflict with Kyiv, providing extensive military equipment and financial support.
President Donald Trump , meanwhile, said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent U.S. military base in the country. "They are friends of mine. They are great people, so we will certainly look at it," Trump said Monday.
Asked about the developments, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that they "cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighboring country cannot," according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security," Peskov said.

The proposed amendment, which will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass, would remove that provision.
Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said scrapping the restriction would bolster the country's resilience and remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other EU and NATO countries.
"We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us," Olekas said, according to state broadcaster LRT .
"By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," he added.

Image source, Bell County Sheriff's Office/Reuters
Image caption, An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that US defence secretary Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Parnell said the secretary of the US Army would set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Watch: Why is America running out of execution drugs? , external
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
Figure caption, How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

items.title: France's Mistral launches AI model it says outperforms some Chinese rivals - Reuters
items.summary: France's Mistral launches AI model it says outperforms some Chinese rivals  Reuters
items.content:
In the spring of 2025, eleven EU health ministers described Europe’s dependence on Chinese medicines as the weak point in Europe’s defense. The warning was accurate but largely ignored. For twenty of fifty-six active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) that German regulators classify as essential to supply, enough of the world’s production sits in China that a disruption there would leave European patients without ready alternatives [PDF].
The more troubling dependency lies one layer down. An ingredient made in India or Europe is still made from something, and those chemical building blocks are more heavily concentrated in China than the ingredients themselves. For metformin, a widely prescribed diabetes drug, roughly one-third of supply is exposed to a disruption in China at the ingredient stage. Count the building block that ingredient is made from, and the figure surpasses four-fifths. The antibiotics amoxicillin and cefpodoxime follow the same pattern. Europe can buy its ingredients from non-Chinese manufacturers and remain dependent on China all the same.
Europe inflicted this damage on itself. These dependencies are the result of decades of cost containment in European health systems, which squeezed margins on generic drugs until production left the continent. China, in turn, undertook an equally deliberate industrial policy to build the capacity Europe had shed.
In April 2026, Washington put additional pressure on the EU by announcing tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports of patented medicines and their ingredients, with European products capped at 15 percent. Generic drugs are exempt for now but will be subject to a review due within a year. Europe therefore faces a strategic question with a short fuse: whether to build resilience alone or with partners—and if with partners, on what terms. Partnership is the stronger choice, but on terms that leave Europe’s own pricing, procurement, and regulatory decisions untouched.
Three features of the drug dependency problem make a transatlantic answer more compelling than a purely European one. First, the exposure is shared, and it sits upstream. The U.S. Commerce Department’s investigation found that only around 15 percent of patented APIs by volume are made in the United States. On antibiotics, the concentration is even starker: China supplied roughly 70 percent [PDF] of U.S. antibiotic ingredient imports by volume in 2024, reversing the position of European producers, who held three-quarters of that market in the early 1990s. Neither Europe nor the United States is dealing with a national vulnerability. They are dealing with the same chokepoint, at the same layer of the value chain, in the same molecules.
Second, Europe holds assets that other regions do not. The last large-scale, fully integrated penicillin production site in the Western world is in Austria; the United States has no domestic capacity for making penicillin ingredients or their core precursor. In biologics, or medications that come from living organisms, Europe, along with North America, dominates not only the manufacture of biological ingredients but also the wider production system behind them: the engineered cell lines that produce the drug molecule, the nutrient mixtures those cells grow in, and the chemical solutions that keep the product stable while it is purified. Chinese and Indian producers are still catching up in that segment. Europe can therefore approach Washington as a supplier or co-supplier of security, not a supplicant for it.
Third, unilateral onshoring on both sides is self-defeating, and the current U.S. measures are counterproductive. Europe is the only ally with the penicillin capacity Washington lacks. Tariffs on European medicines raise costs across that base. Extending the regime to generic drugs, which the pending review could do, would reach the most fragile part of European production, where every plant closure is a market share transfer to China. The political effect is worse than the commercial one. Each coercive measure against Europe drains support in European capitals for the transatlantic option and strengthens the argument that resilience should mean autonomy from everyone. If the United States’ objective is an allied answer to Chinese dominance, current instruments are producing the opposite result.
The terms of cooperation matter from Europe’s perspective as well. A strategy that trades one dependency for another is not resilience. Several instruments now on the table in Washington would do exactly that: tariff relief conditioned on relocating production to the United States, drug-pricing commitments negotiated company by company under tariff pressure, and procurement rules with extraterritorial reach [PDF] that determine which suppliers European firms may use. Europe should cooperate on capacity, information, and standards, while retaining sovereign control over pricing, procurement, and regulatory decisions. Any proposal must meet a simple test: if the partnership broke down, Europe must still be able to supply its patients.
Europe and the United States should begin where cooperation costs nothing politically. They could start by fixing their lack of visibility into their own upstream flows of key starting materials. Joint mapping, which builds on the work of the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority and its U.S. counterparts, is a technical exercise that produces shared information and nothing else. It changes no tariff, no procurement rule, and no market access, so neither side has to concede anything to take part. They should also undertake joint stress-testing on a shared methodology that measures not just how much production sits in China but how long replacement would take if production stopped. In particular, NATO should incorporate the defense-relevant subset of the stress-testing—demand for antibiotics, analgesics, and anesthetics under mobilization conditions—into its resilience work.
Europe should also lock in the existing carve-out under the 2025 United States-European Union Framework —which already grants near-zero treatment to generic medicines, their ingredients, and chemical precursors—and press to make it permanent, including for biosimilars, the lower-cost follow-on versions of biologic drugs whose patents have expired, before the U.S. review of generics concludes.
Europe should legislate its own rules on sensitive biotech and health-data cooperation with China rather than importing American ones through contractual reach. But the U.S. approach warrants careful study. In principle, a plurilateral critical-medicines arrangement modeled on the allied approach now emerging for critical raw materials would make sense. That would include giving preferential treatment to ally-produced ingredients and precursors, mutually recognizing the validity of the other side’s inspections, and establishing common resilience criteria in public procurement. The United States and Europe should establish such a framework with India, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, among others. The idea would be to coordinate demand: agreeing to long-term purchase commitments that give investors enough certainty to finance new Western production. The binding constraint on that capacity is not technology but price, with European ingredients running up to 40 percent more than Chinese ones. Only guaranteed demand closes that gap. Currently, however, transatlantic relations lack the trust required for such a comprehensive plurilateral arrangement.
The United States’ and Europe’s dependency on Chinese pharmaceutical ingredients was built over decades, and it will not be undone quickly. Europe should start with what can be done now: mapping the upstream flows neither side can currently see, testing how long replacement would actually take, and locking in the generics carve-out before the review closes it. None of that requires trust that does not exist. All of it would make a larger arrangement possible later, if the politics allow.
What Europe should not do is trade away control over its own pharmaceutical market to gain access to America’s. The purpose of reducing dependence on China is to widen Europe’s room to maneuver, not to narrow it again from a different direction. Washington should recognize that each tariff on European medicines cuts against the very alliance it says it wants.
This report was informed by a Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) meeting convened in cooperation with the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS) as part of a project on transatlantic cooperation on China policy. The author thanks the members of the Council on Foreign Relations working group on transatlantic cooperation for the discussion from which this brief emerged, and Martin Catarata, David Francas, Jasmina Kirchhoff and Fearghal Raison, his coauthors on the underlying study. That study, Strategische Abhängigkeiten bei wichtigen Arzneimitteln von China , was conducted at the German Economic Institute and commissioned by Pro Generika, the German generics association. The views expressed here are the author’s own.

Rebounding Hormuz oil exports vulnerable to increased Iranian attacks
Crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz have increased but only due to a major U.S. military commitment and at a high cost to the lives of tanker crews.
Iran, meanwhile, is stepping up its attacks on tankers.
The rebound in exports may be unsustainable in the absence of a negotiated settlement or capitulation by Tehran.
Iran has stepped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, threatening a fragile rebound of crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf.
Nearly 20 commercial ships, mostly tankers, have come under attack over the past month while sailing through Hormuz, the Persian Gulf or off the coast of Oman, according to the Joint Maritime Information Center , a group of U.S.-allied militaries that provide security updates to merchant vessels.
Iran attacked roughly two ships for every 100 vessels that crossed the strait in the third quarter, said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, which tracks ships for defense departments and governments.
Oil flows through Hormuz now depend on a major U.S. military commitment to protect tankers transiting along a southern route along the coast of Oman.
With the security situation in Hormuz still dangerous, it is unclear how long the rebound in crude exports can be sustained in the absence of a negotiated settlement or capitulation by Tehran.
In many cases, tankers are bringing crude through Hormuz and then transferring the oil onto ships in the Gulf of Oman that haul it to Asia. This shuttle system reduces the exposure to attack from Iran but also requires more vessels to move the oil.
"Nobody in Washington thinks this is sustainable financially," said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush, referring to the U.S. military commitment in the Gulf, ship-to-ship transfers and heightened tanker rates. "It's an inefficient way to move commodities, not just oil, out of Hormuz," McNally said.
Crude oil shipments through Hormuz fluctuate daily, sometimes matching or even exceeding levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler, a firm that tracks tankers and global trade flows.
At other times, exports are lower than volumes seen before the conflict. Shipments averaged about 10.3 million barrels per day for the week ended Saturday, about 23% below a prewar baseline of 13.5 million bpd, according to Kpler data published Monday.
Windward estimates crude through Hormuz is averaging 9-10 million bpd compared with a prewar baseline of 14.5 million bpd.
While crude flows are volatile, they have ramped up compared with earlier in the war as the U.S. military has successfully carved out the shipping route along Oman's coast, analysts say.
But shippers are ferrying crude through Hormuz at high cost to the lives of their crews and in freight and insurance rates, Bockmann said. Since July, at least nine sailors have died, 18 injured and three are missing, according to the International Maritime Organization , a United Nations agency.
"Volumes are getting through but they're getting through at a time of extremely high maritime risk," Bockmann said. As security has deteriorated, the cost of shipping crude from the Persian Gulf to China has skyrocketed to $1 million per day for each tanker.
"Oil flows have recovered because the market participants have accepted greater operational complexity and higher costs," said Richard Meade, editor in chief of Lloyd's List, a London-based maritime industry trade publication, in a briefing last Thursday.
But the threat to tankers remains the same, Meade said. Brent oil prices, the international benchmark, are still hovering near $100 per barrel, even as more crude makes it out of Hormuz.
"If the market believed that this was sustainable, I think you would be seeing much lower prices," McNally at Rapidan said. Prices remain high because "it's still costly to deliver and insure and land crude in consuming regions where benchmark prices are set," he said.
And while more oil is getting out, freedom of navigation in Hormuz has not been restored, McNally said. Tehran continues to insist that it controls the strait.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Monday hailed down a tanker transiting the strait and ordered the ship to turn around or face attack, according to an incident report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. The vessel complied.
"The oil market is not becoming more secure," Meade said. "It is becoming more efficient at operating under sustained insecurity."

items.title: OpenAI and Synopsys partner to build "GPT-Synopsys" for autonomous chip design — specialized AI model will operate EDA tools, allowing engineers to deliver more sophisticated chips faster - Tom's Hardware
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
OpenAI and Synopsys have signed a multi-year agreement to jointly develop GPT-Synopsys, a specialized model optimized for semiconductor design using Synopsys's electronic design automation (EDA) tools. According to the September 30 announcement , the partnership "brings together OpenAI's advanced AI capabilities with Synopsys's industry-leading EDA tools and agentic AI capabilities to revolutionize the design of semiconductors."
Engineers would delegate to agents that run the tools and execute the required processes until the work is ready for review. The companies say this would allow design teams to evaluate more options and deliver more sophisticated chips. Under the preferred partner agreement, OpenAI is licensing Synopsys's tools to develop the model — which will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure — after which the companies will jointly release the product and share revenue. The announcement did not disclose a release date or a pricing structure.
Engineers use EDA tools to design and verify chips before manufacturing. This multi-step process begins with writing the hardware description in register-transfer level (RTL) code and using synthesis software to convert it into logic gates. Next, physical design tools lay out the circuit elements and route the connections between them. Lastly, designers close timing, verify functionality, and ensure manufacturing compliance before tapeout for fabrication.
Each of these stages requires several iterations — repeatedly running various tools and troubleshooting issues — to balance critical trade-offs: power, performance, and silicon area (PPA). Synopsys, Cadence, and Siemens EDA have dominated this market for these tools long before the current AI boom. Given the technology's capabilities, it is only natural that AI has found its way into the chip design process , creating a sort of "silicon designing silicon" loop.
In March 2020, Synopsys launched DSO.ai (Design Space Optimization AI), a reinforcement learning tool that explores and learns from previous design optimizations to improve PPA. The company then launched Synopsys.ai Copilot in November 2023 — its first integration of generative AI — through a collaboration with Microsoft , integrating the Azure OpenAI service to provide natural language assistance within its engineering tools.
The company's current direction is Agentic AI, first revealed at the Design Automation Conference in July, where it showed an autonomous verification workflow built on Nvidia's Agent Toolkit and Nemotron 3 Ultra model. On September 28, two days before the OpenAI deal, Synopsys announced its Autopilot platform and AgentEngineer , a portfolio of seven long-horizon agents covering verification, implementation, analog, manufacturing, meshing, combustion, and EMC analysis. The company reported more than 50 engagements, with availability planned for late 2026.
As detailed in our State of agentic AI in chip design tools roadmap, the move to agentic AI is not exclusive to Synopsys; Cadence and Siemens are also pitching autonomous design agents. Meanwhile, OpenAI, in collaboration with Broadcom, unveiled Jalapeño in June, the company's first custom inference accelerator. OpenAI said the accelerator's design and optimization process leaned heavily on its AI models , allowing it to go from initial design to tape-out in just nine months. Now, GPT-Synopsys turns that internal experiment into a product.
According to the announcement, GPT-Synopsys will combine OpenAI's frontier models with Synopsys's EDA software and domain expertise, allowing the model to reason about chip design and verification and operate Synopsys tools directly. Engineers would hand the model objectives such as PPA optimization, timing, and verification closure, while the agents run the tools, interpret the results, implement changes, and iterate toward verified outcomes for an engineer to review.
In other words, the model would be capable of making engineering judgments involved in using Synopsys software. The companies describe it as learning to operate the tools like an expert engineer, interpreting their outputs and using the results to guide further changes. This is the proposed specialization that takes the model beyond connecting a general-purpose model to a set of tools.
Synopsys's EDA engines would perform the calculations and checks, with the model interpreting results and the agent software managing execution. GPT-Synopsys will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure and is intended to integrate with Synopsys.ai and Autopilot, as well as work with customers' own agent harnesses. Autopilot already provides services such as memory and governance.
Synopsys says early technology engagements are underway with leading semiconductor customers, but didn't name any. The immediate audience is professional semiconductor-design teams, with companies developing their own custom silicon also likely to use it. Although the announcement covers semiconductor design generally, OpenAI has a particular interest in improving the hardware that runs its models. "By helping them build better chips, we can build better AI and bring it to more people," said Greg Brockman, OpenAI's president and co-founder. Whether the service also makes advanced design more accessible to smaller teams will depend on pricing and the expertise still required to supervise it.
The recent announcement leaves a couple of questions and concerns unaddressed. First, hosting the model on OpenAI infrastructure raises concerns about how confidential designs are handled. The companies say customer data will be excluded from model training, encrypted at rest and in transit, and governed by configurable retention, audit, and permission controls. However, the release does not identify hosting regions or default retention periods. It also provides no contractual terms for ownership of generated outputs, use of third-party licensed design IP, or indemnities. The service's terms will likely address these questions.
Another question is the practical economics for users. The industry has realized that handing over everything to AI doesn't always result in cost savings , at least for now. Sometimes the reverse is the case. Earlier this year, Uber's CTO and an Nvidia executive said AI was more expensive than human workers , although many companies are reportedly fine with the extra cost. For GPT-Synopsys, advanced engineering reasoning and faster design-to-tapeout could justify the service, but model calls, EDA runs, integration, and human review all consume resources. The announcement did not include a pricing structure. It also didn't specify a launch date.
Meanwhile, Synopsys's main rival Cadence launched its ChipStack AI Super Agent in February for front-end design and verification, built on frontier LLMs. In April, the company announced a collaboration with Google to optimize ChipStack with Gemini on Google Cloud. At Computex , it extended ChipStack to what it calls Level-5 autonomy, powered by Nvidia's Nemotron models, with early access expected in the second half of 2026. The main difference is that while ChipStack is Cadence's own agent software running on other companies' general-purpose models, GPT-Synopsys will be an OpenAI model specifically trained to operate Synopsys's tools.
Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

U.S. calls for transparency on reported Russian plague death
Oct. 6, 2026, 9:01 AM EDT  /  Updated   Oct. 6, 2026, 3:58 PM EDT
Plague had not been detected among close contacts of a worker in an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia who died last week, with 60% of the identified group tested so far, officials in Russia said Tuesday.
News from Russia’s consumer and health watchdog on Sunday that a female staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin last week has raised public health fears worldwide.
“Laboratory testing identified two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection,” watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement, referring to the virus that causes the common cold. “No other infectious disease pathogens were detected among the contacts,” the statement said, without mentioning the word “plague.”
Darya Shipilova, 28, was identified by her mother and Russian media outlets as the lab worker who died.
Regional and national Russian authorities have not confirmed that plague was involved in her death. However, a State Department spokesperson said Monday there had been “reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague” in Irkutsk oblast.
Lab workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, in an undated photo. via AP Separately, a State Department official told NBC News on Tuesday that the U.S. had been in contact with the Russian government as early as Friday. Health experts at the State Department had taken part in the contact along with the Russian Foreign Ministry, the official said.
The Centers for Disease Control & Prevention also said on X that it was “working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available.”

No case of plague or other high threat pathogen has reportedly been found among the woman’s close contacts, the WHO said, quoting the response from the Russian officials, adding that it’s awaiting confirmation from the Russian side about “what pneumonia-causing pathogen had led to the individual’s death.”
On Friday, Maksim Modin, mayor of the Shelekhov municipal district near the border with Mongolia, said that the inpatient facility where the worker is said to have been treated had been closed for quarantine. Russian media cited officials saying that nearly 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under precautionary medical observation.
Russian media outlets have named the woman and identified her as being 28 years old. These details have not been announced by officials.
Irkutsk’s governor, Igor Kobsev, said Monday that no “microorganisms linked to the employee’s professional activities were detected” in her body.
The Irkutsk regional branch of Rospotrebnadzor on Tuesday denied what it called “fake” reports circulating online that an “enhanced sanitary-epidemiological regime” and strict restrictions have been imposed in the region.
“No such decisions have been made at this time,” it said in a statement, saying the situation in the region remains stable.

Igor Ivanko / AFP via Getty Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that even though there is “very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia,” if “something like that gets out, it could quickly spread.”
Rospotrebnadzor, the health watchdog, said Tuesday its probe found “no incidents involving the handling of pathogenic microorganisms.”
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday the United States would do what it could to help Russia.
“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “It’s a rough disease.”
Meanwhile, some of Russia’s neighbors have been stepping up preventive measures and quarantine controls at border crossings.
The Kremlin has called for those concerned to heed official statements.

On its website, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East says it was founded in 1934 “as a scientific and operational body for combating plague,” but over the years, its scope of responsibility expanded to include “other highly dangerous diseases,” including cholera and anthrax.
The institute says it’s a “multidisciplinary research and anti-epidemic facility” that helps ensure epidemic safety in the region.

items.title: Californians blast Trump remark that Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles, San Diego - Reuters
items.summary: Californians blast Trump remark that Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles, San Diego  Reuters
items.content:
Figure caption, Trump on Iran: 'Let them take out LA, let them take out San Diego'
By Jamie Whitehead   and   Bernd Debusmann Jr ,  White House reporter
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.
California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."
There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.
The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.
In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".
"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".
The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.
A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.
"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.
San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.
Image caption, Trump and Newsom met when the president visited California in January after the state was hit by wildfires
This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.
Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.
Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.
Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

items.content:
Image caption, US televangelist Jim Bakker's death was announced on Monday by his second wife Lori Bakker
US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar media empire before being jailed for fraud and conspiracy, has died aged 86.
Bakker and his then-wife Tammy Faye founded a Christian television programme called The PTL Club in 1974, which at its peak attracted 13 million viewers per day.
The 86-year-old's death was announced on Monday by his second wife Lori Bakker, who described him as "a pioneer of Christian television".
By the late 80s, Bakker and Tammy Faye's empire began to fall apart after he became embroiled in a sex scandal and later convicted of mail and wire fraud. Tammy Faye, who divorced him in 1992, was never charged.
Bakker remarried in 1998, and alongside second wife Lori launched a new TV ministry in 2003.
Lori Bakker described her late husband as "my best friend, and the man I was honoured to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry".
However, Bakker's first program The PTL Club - short for 'Praise the Lord' or 'People That Love' - was what cemented his fame with his first wife Tammy Faye.
The couple built their empire with 2,000 employees and a 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA theme park complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
The Bakkers had a famously opulent lifestyle, owning a private jet, multiple homes, luxury cars, jewellery and even an air-conditioned dog house.
In 1987, Bakker resigned from the PTL ministry after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with a former church secretary Jessica Hahn.
It later emerged Hanhn received a $265,000 payoff with ministry funds, resulting in Bakker being defrocked of his ministerial credentials and right to perform religious duties.
Image caption, Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker had a famously opulent lifestyle, owning a private jet, multiple homes and luxury cars
Hahn also accused Bakker of sexual assault, though the evangelist denied this, claiming the encounter had been consensual.
Bakker was then convicted in 1989 of 24 counts of mail and wire fraud and conspiracy in a scheme involving their Christian theme park, and served more than four years in prison.
Tammy Faye stayed with her husband throughout the trial but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.
Following Bakker's release from prison in 1994, he wrote a book titled I Was Wrong and married his second wife Lori in 1998.
The couple began a TV ministry together in 2003 and in 2008 they began taping The Jim Bakker Show.

items.summary: Tobias Rausch secures role of president in Saxony-Anhalt after AfD’s election breakthroughEurope live – latest updatesAlternative für Deutschland has become Germany’s first far-right party to secure the position of speaker of a regional parliament since the second world war.Tobias Rausch, a fo
items.content:
Ulrich Siegmund, right, congratulates Tobias Rausch on becoming president of the federal state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday. Both represent Germany’s far-right AfD party. Photograph: Jan Woitas/Pool DPA/AP
Ulrich Siegmund, right, congratulates Tobias Rausch on becoming president of the federal state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday. Both represent Germany’s far-right AfD party. Photograph: Jan Woitas/Pool DPA/AP
State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war
Tobias Rausch secures role of president in Saxony-Anhalt after AfD’s election breakthrough
Alternative für Deutschland has become Germany’s first far-right party to secure the position of speaker of a regional parliament since the second world war.
Tobias Rausch, a former estate agent, was elected in the first round of voting on Tuesday in Saxony-Anhalt. He won 48 out of the 82 votes cast.
Later in the day, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, part of the AfD’s more extreme wing, was elected as Rausch’s deputy.
The AfD, which is classed as “rightwing extremist” by the eastern state’s intelligence agency, won nearly 44% of votes in elections last month , dealing a hammer blow to Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU).
Rausch’s election to the role of president of the parliament – and its speaker – took place at the inaugural gathering of members in the state capital, Magdeburg. Twenty-nine voted against Rausch and five abstained.
Protesters console each other outside the state parliament in Magdeburg after the election of Tobias Rausch as speaker on Tuesday. Photograph: Maja Hitij/Getty Images The AfD parliamentary group holds 39 seats, narrowly short of an absolute majority. Five politicians from the BSW, a small leftwing party that echoes the AfD’s stances on Russia and immigration, had already said they would vote for Rausch. Tuesday’s result means that four other MPs voted for the 35-year-old in the secret ballot.
The willingness of politicians to break the “firewall” – a moral agreement among other parties to shun the AfD – gives the party a chance of being able to form a government in the state – a feat it had looked unlikely to pull off. This would be even more of a historical watershed in postwar Germany.
The BSW’s support for Rausch came after the party’s founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, declared it was time to do away with “firewall idiocy”. The party’s deputy leader, Christian Leye, said the “firewall is not working” and the votes of nearly 44% of electors could not be ignored.
“We need an intelligent way of dealing with the AfD and that means dealing with the content of their programme instead of a firewall,” Leye told German media.
Hans-Thomas Tillschneider in the state parliament after being elected deputy speaker on Tuesday. He is being lined up as Saxony-Anhalt’s culture and science minister. Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/Reuters It was not immediately clear who was behind Tillschneider’s election because the BSW had said it would refuse to vote for him. He received 44 votes.
As the architect of the AfD’s “radical” manifesto, he is lined up to become culture and science minister in the state. He has referred to the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as “a real man with a sound set of values” and accused immigrants of “streaming in here in masses … wanting to squander our money”.
Tillschneider is a scholar of Islamic studies who has described Islam as a “fungus” growing on the “German oak”. His family emigrated from Romania to Germany in the 1980s.
In his acceptance speech, Rausch promised to represent all voices and “take different opinions seriously and to try to take decisions in a transparent way”. He was applauded by his own parliamentary group and the ranks of the BSW. The other MPs did not respond.
Demonstrators read the German constitution during a protest outside Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament on Tuesday. Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty Images Rausch was one of the key figures in a nepotism scandal over AfD MPs employing family members in parliament. He denied claims that several of his siblings and a brother-in-law were working in the state parliament but confirmed he was employing several players from the football club where he is a member.
He is a close ally and confidant of Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, who is positioning himself to take over as leader of Saxony-Anhalt. He has yet to say which parties or politicians have agreed to cooperate with the AfD, only that “negotiations are going well”. The AfD claims to be courting members of the CDU to break the firewall, a claim CDU leaders deny.
The BSW says it will support an AfD-led parliament only if a nonpartisan figure is appointed to lead it, a position the AfD rejects. Siegmund has until December to form a government.
Opposition MPs raised alarm over the breaching of the firewall. “Whoever has invested a representative of extremist and anti-constitutional party with this office will bear responsibility for the consequences,” said Green MP Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, to loud applause.
The result of the Saxony-Anhalt poll, along with two other regional elections in September, has piled huge pressure on Merz, who pledged on taking office in 2025 that he would halve the AfD’s support by boosting the economy and reducing immigration. Instead, the CDU’s support has more or less halved and that of the AfD has surged to 30% in national polls.
Before the vote, Eva von Angern of the leftwing Die Linke party and the longest-serving member of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament, drew parallels between Rausch’s election to the post of speaker, and Hermann Göring’s use of that role in the Reichstag in the 1930s to facilitate Adolf Hitler’s rise to power.
She claimed that the negative consequences of the AfD’s win in the state were already being felt in lower tourist numbers and teachers withdrawing job applications.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says Investors Should Make This Important Move - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says Investors Should Make This Important Move  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says Investors Should Make This Important Move
The last few years have been potentially life-changing for stock market investors. And you didn't need to do anything particularly complicated to earn massive returns. Just betting on the major indexes would have been enough, with the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) soaring by roughly 80% and 91%, respectively, over the last five years alone.
Much of this growth has been driven by optimism surrounding generative AI . But what goes up often eventually comes back down. And there are growing signs that sentiment could be shifting, with analysts at consulting firm Capital Economics expecting the "bubble" to begin to burst in 2027. Let's discuss how Warren Buffett's lessons could help investors navigate this increasingly uncertain stock market environment.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Capital Economics believes AI will be transformative and increase company profits, but the research firm doesn't think the benefits will be as high as many analysts expect. And it isn't the only one getting nervous about the party ending soon. Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Jan Hatzius also recently warned that the AI investment boom won't last forever.
Global AI-related capital spending is expected to hit $1 trillion in 2026. And if this spending cycle dries up, it could directly lead to less revenue and profits for the hardware providers like Nvidia and Micron Technology , which have contributed to much of the stock market's recent growth.
Regular people are also seeing the writing on the wall through popular stock market valuation tools like the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio. This metric compares stock prices with average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last decade to provide a view of how expensive the market is relative to other points in history. And it now stands at 41.3. That's far above its average of 17.4 and a level that hasn't been seen since the late '90s dot-com bubble, when it hit a peak of 44.
Rising interest rates and bond yields also aren't helping the situation, because they increase the cost of capital while making risky tech stocks look less attractive relative to holding government debt.
Throughout his over six-decade-long investing career, Buffett had to navigate plenty of booms and busts in the stock market. His success has been attributed to a unique yet simple investing strategy that focuses on long-term holding and sustainable value creation. Buffett's quotes from the dot-com bubble era are particularly relevant for investors navigating a similar situation right now.
In 2000, he famously urged technology investors to be cautious after the huge returns they enjoyed in 1998 and 1999.
Image source: The Motley Fool. "After a heady experience of that kind," he said, "normally sensible people drift into behavior akin to that of Cinderella at the ball. They know that overstaying the festivities ... will eventually bring on pumpkins and mice."
And he was correct. By the end of 2000, the market had fallen 9.1%, before dropping 11.9% in 2001 and 22.1% in 2002. Many of the hardest-hit technology stocks fared much worse -- going bankrupt or taking decades to regain their all-time highs achieved during the bubble.
It is important to note that Warren Buffett didn't sell everything during the dot-com bubble, even though he suspected a big crash was on the horizon. He generally believes that time in the market is a better long-term strategy than trying to time the market because it is difficult to know exactly when a crash will occur or how long it will last.
Investors can imitate Buffett by betting on fairly valued companies with stable, established business models instead of chasing the next big hype cycle. If nothing catches your eye, don't be afraid to sit on cash. Right now, Buffett's investment firm, Berkshire Hathaway , has $365.5 billion in liquidity, putting it in an excellent position to shop for deals if market valuations get cheaper over the next few months.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Photo: SCMP)
South African exporters are sending increased shipments of bulk raw materials to East Asia after China launched a zero-tariff policy for African exports.
The duty-free framework, effective from May 1, 2026, aims to boost industrialization and balanced trade, excluding Eswatini due to its ties with Taiwan.
Exports of key commodities like chrome, magnetite, iron ore, and corn have surged through South Africa's Port of Ngqura.
Port officials report exponential growth in cargo volumes bound for China, driven by strong demand and favorable prices.

The two-year zero-tariff policy, which officially took effect on May 1, 2026, covers qualifying exports from all African nations (excluding Eswatini due to its cordial relationship with Taiwan ) in order to support regional industrialization and balanced trade.
Shipments of key commodities, including chrome, magnetite, iron ore, and corn, have surged through South Africa’s deep-water Port of Ngqura in the Eastern Cape Province.
South African commodity exports boom under China's duty-free policy
Port management reports substantial growth in freight volume moving toward Chinese industrial hubs.
Xola Mkontwana, business strategy manager at the Port of Ngqura, revealed that the logistics center experienced " exponential growth " in cargo destined for the Chinese market.
As reported by Xinhua, the strategist explained that "the zero-tariff has assisted the throughput for bulk across the port system because there's chrome and magnetite, iron ore, and also corn".
Addressing the drivers behind this surge in trade, Mkontwana pointed to rapid industrial and infrastructure growth in China alongside lucrative prices for African agricultural and mining businesses .
He observed , "It's the market that is there and the price that is good for the miners and owners".
China expands zero tariffs to Africa while the U.S. raises import duties and cuts foreign aid
While China broadens trade access for African commodities, relations between the United States and several African nations face deepening trade and diplomatic friction.
The Trump administration enacted a 12.5% tariff on affected imports from South Africa, Nigeria, and five other African economies on July 24 after completing a Section 301 investigation.
U.S. President Donald Trump .[Image Credit: Bloomberg/Getty Images ]
Washington issued a "stop-work" order across foreign aid initiatives to review whether overseas funding aligns with U.S. foreign policy priorities.
In South Africa, Washington announced plans to phase out roughly $400 million in annual HIV/AIDS support funded through the PEPFAR initiative.
According to Business Insider Africa, a U.S. State Department official stated that the decision aims to "promote self-reliance and reduce dependence on American assistance," asserting that South Africa's middle-income status allows it to take on greater financial responsibility for national health programs.
Aparently, Beijing's zero-tariff policy draws African economies closer by opening trade opportunities just as U.S. tariffs and aid withdrawals create new trade huddles across the continent.

Fuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on
Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers
Fuel is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals.
“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine .”
British armed forces intercept Russian shadow fleet oil tanker in Channel
Seoul has sent Ukraine humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies such as helmets, body armour and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.
But South Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.
While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law. South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyiv come under strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show.
The largest carrier, the sanctioned Layla , made two voyages from the south-eastern port of Ulsan to Vladivostok leaving on 19 July and 10 August and carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities its destination was Vladivostok, but on the second it said it was bound for Niigata in Japan.
Korea-Russia map Another sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flagged Astoria , which is also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August, declaring Japan as its destination, before sailing to Vladivostok.
Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border
The third sanctioned tanker, the Chongchon , never berthed. It took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from an unsanctioned tanker, the Celeste I, at an anchorage off the southern South Korean port of Yeosu in early August, then headed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.
The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment.
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.
According to data from the maritime analytics firm Kpler, the buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is under UK, US, EU and Australian sanctions , and NNK, a Russian oil group whose owner, Eduard Khudainatov , and one of its companies, NNK-Oil, are under UK sanctions.
In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India.
Loadings at South Korean ports began to surge in July, just as the country’s president, Lee Jae Myung, pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a Nato summit in Turkey.
A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade.
In March, as the war with Iran shut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver.
On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG that takes effect in January 2027.
When contacted, South Korea’s foreign ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”
It said it had expanded its export controls on Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.
The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.
The UK Foreign Office did not answer questions about the UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, or say whether the shipments had been raised with Seoul.
A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.”

items.content:
A trader on the stock exchange floor. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters
A trader on the stock exchange floor. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters
S&P 500 and Nasdaq surge to record highs after AI chipmaker rally
S&P tops 7,800 for first time in history as investors optimistic despite signs of instability in US economy
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at a record high after a rally around AI chipmakers and a dip in US treasury yields.
At market’s close, the S&P 500 was up 0.58%, topping 7,800 for the first time in its history. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose 0.45%, while the Dow, which is slightly down from its record high in August, climbed 0.49%.
Investors appeared optimistic after recent developments for chipmakers including Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom that showed growth in the markets for the chips used to power AI.
Wall Street has also grown more optimistic that the US Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its next board meeting in October. Job figures from September showed underwhelming growth in the labor market, and multiple Fed officials have said the next interest rate increase can probably wait.
The optimism in the stock market, largely coming from continuing investment in AI, has defied other signs of instability in the US economy and global politics.
The US bond market, typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, has been in turmoil in recent weeks. US bond yields, or the return an investor receives when a bond matures, reached recent highs amid concerns over high inflation and interest rates. The yield for 10-year US treasury bonds on Monday reached 5.349%, the highest since April 2022, before dipping back down on Tuesday.
For American consumers, higher energy prices continue to be a major pain point. While gas prices have dipped over the last week, prices are still about $1.20 a gallon on average higher than a year ago. Diesel, which is used to fuel trucks, buses and trains, has also gone down from record high but is still over 40% higher than a year ago.
The economy is expected to be a top issue in the upcoming midterm elections, with many voters expressing frustration over high prices. Donald Trump, who has been stumping for Republican candidates across the country, has been trying to paint a different picture for voters.
At a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump said that “our nation is doing better now than it’s ever done” and that gas prices would fall below $1.85 a gallon “in no time”.

items.summary: Interest rate hikes create winners and losers in Lehigh Valley economy  Lehigh Valley Business
items.content:
Interest rate hikes create winners and losers in Lehigh Valley economy
Interest rate hikes create winners and losers in Lehigh Valley economy
Going against expectations and political pressures, the U.S. Federal Reserve in September raised its benchmark federal funds rate a quarter point to a target range to 3.75%-4.00%.
The move was designed to combat elevated inflation and support a return to the Federal Reserve's 2% inflation goal.
The Fed also indicated that more rate increases could be in the future.
While he said the Fed sticking to its policies despite political pressures is a good sign that the reserve is being well managed, Ahmed Rahman, a research fellow at the Institute of Labor Economics at Lehigh University in Bethlehem, said there are sure to be winners and losers with any trend in interest rates. And, he said, the Lehigh Valley is a good example of how the economy will be impacted on both a micro and macro level.
“Spenders are going to see the benefit while borrowers are going to be negatively impacted,” Rahman said.
There is a demographic component to the issue, he said.
“Older people, who hopefully have savings, this will give them bigger savings,” he said. “Young people who tend to be borrowers will be spending more.”
He also said different regions will see a different impact from any rate hike depending on demographics.
“The Lehigh Valley has an average mix compared to other parts of the country,” he said that makes the region a good example of how interest rates impact a community.
“For the first time homeowner, it's going to be harder, Rahman said. “Buying a home right now is already difficult and this isn't making it any easier.”
And it's not just the mortgage rates that will impact the residential real estate market.
“The interest rate increase will stifle new home construction putting less homes on the market,” he said.
The Lehigh Valley will be highly impacted by this, he said, because the region has relatively lower housing costs than surrounding regions like New York, New Jersey and the Philadelphia region.
Those getting priced out of those areas will become more likely to look for homes in the Lehigh Valley, a move that will lessen inventory and increase prices.
From an employment perspective, Rahman said higher interest rates will have less of an impact, locally.
The Lehigh Valley has a strong health care economy , which is more stable as far as employment goes and less impacted by interest rates.
So even if employers facing higher costs may be laying off employees in some industries, the Lehigh Valley has a buffer because of its high employment in health care.
However, Rahman said many industries will be impacted. Small to medium sized businesses are likely to be hit the hardest because they don't have the economies of scale or access to alternative funding sources that larger companies have.
It might make it harder for small companies to grow organically.
Rahman said he believes that could impact merger and acquisition activity as similar companies seek to join forces to grow their businesses.
So, why was there political pressure to reduce rather than increase the Fed rate?
Rahman said there is a very impactful mid-term election coming up, and lower interest rates are popular with voters.
Lower interest rates, however, are more likely to boost inflation. But since that wouldn't happen until after the election, politicians are more interested in what is happening now not later, Rahman aid.
“I'm excited that were testing the political boundaries,” Rahman said. “One of the key fundamentals of the Fed is its independence and that it can address employment and inflation issues regardless of the political situation.”

items.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
items.summary: Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.
items.content:
Image caption, OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney
By Lana Lam   and   Simon Atkinson ,  Australia producer
OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.
The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.
"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.
Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.
Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.
An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.
When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.
"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.
"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."
Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.
"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."
OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.
The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.
Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.
This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.
The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".
"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."
Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.
"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.
The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.
An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.
"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.
Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

Fed holds interest rates steady as inflation hits 3-year high
Futures markets overwhelmingly expected the Fed to keep rates unchanged.
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday as the economy weathers its highest inflation in three years.
The announcement marked the first decision on interest rates rates since Trump nominee Kevin Warsh took the helm as Fed chair.
Speaking at a press conference, Warsh voiced a commitment to bring inflation down to the Fed's desired level of 2%. The annual pace of price increases currently registers at more than twice that target rate.
"Persistently high prices are a burden for the American people," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C. "This committee will deliver price stability."
All 12 members of the FOMC voted to hold interest rates steady, meaning Warsh and his predecessor, former Fed Chair Jerome Powell, agreed on the rate decision.
Nine members indicated they expect to raise interest rates by the end of the year, marking a significant change in sentiment from a previous projection issued three months earlier.
Iran live updates: Trump, Vance were both signatories on MOU
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), a 12-member policymaking body at the Fed, issued a statement describing inflation as "elevated."
The current level of inflation in part reflects "supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy," the FOMC said.
The policy move also arrived at a moment of flux for the nation’s economy, just days after an agreement between the United States and Iran offered hope for some price relief.
The U.S.-Iran accord, set to be formally signed on Friday, came as gasoline prices fell below $4 a gallon for the first time since March. Still, fuel costs stand well above pre-war levels, and an array of grocery prices remain elevated.
In recent weeks, odds have risen for a potential interest rate hike by the end of 2026, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, which grants a roughly four in 10 chance of a quarter-point increase in December.
The shift in expectations came after a stronger-than-expected jobs report earlier this month showed robust hiring in May. In theory, a resilient labor market could afford central bankers leeway to raise interest rates in an effort to dial back inflation, since elevated borrowing costs risk a hiring slowdown.
